title: False king, false subjects
hook: false the king, false the subjects, false the whole world, and still we love it (Asa di Var, ang 468)

segments.voice: Yesterday, cartloads of books, and your line: one thing counts. What did you already know but hadn't lived yet? Today Guru Nanak looks at everything else we count, and gives it a hard name. Day five hundred forty-eight.

Old cities are full of the leftovers of someone's empire. A gate that once had guards. A palace that is now a museum, with a gift shop where the throne room used to be. Whoever built it surely meant it to stand forever. In Guru Nanak's own lifetime, Punjab watched one ruling house fall and another rise: the Lodi sultans gave way to Babur and the Mughals. Guru Nanak saw power change hands up close. And in the Asa di Var there is a salok that starts with the king himself and works its way down to everything we own and love.
screen: `A PALACE WITH A GIFT SHOP.` → `THRONES CHANGE HANDS.` → `A SALOK THAT STARTS WITH THE KING.`

segments.voice: The word that repeats is koorh, and it runs through the salok on ang 468, phrase after phrase. In paraphrase: koorh is the king, koorh the subjects, koorh the whole world. Koorh are the mansions and palaces, and koorh the ones who live in them. Koorh is gold, koorh is silver, koorh are those who wear them. Koorh is the body, koorh the clothes, koorh the matchless beauty. Koorh is the husband, koorh the wife; they waste away and are gone. Koorh usually gets translated false. But in this salok it means something gentler and sadder than lying. It means what passes. What looks solid and isn't. Gold is real gold, a palace is a real palace, and a marriage is a real marriage, but none of them can hold you up forever. Then comes the turn: and still we love it. The false, the salok says, fall in love with the false and forget the Creator. With whom should we make friends? The whole world is passing away. Falsehood is sweet, falsehood is honey; falsehood drowns boatloads of people. And the salok ends with Nanak's plea to the One: without you, everything is koorh, koorh. Sikh teachers are careful here. Guru Nanak, as Sikhs remember him, was a householder who married, raised a family, and in his later years farmed at Kartarpur. Sikhs aren't asked to leave the world or despise it. The point is where the heart leans its full weight. Love your people, use the silver, live in the house. Just don't mistake any of it for the thing that lasts.
screen: `KOORH: KING, SUBJECTS, WORLD.` · `PALACES, GOLD, BEAUTY, MARRIAGE.` · `KOORH MEANS WHAT PASSES.` · `LIVE IN IT; DON'T LEAN ON IT.` · then, large: `WITHOUT YOU, ALL IS KOORH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one thing that won't last. Look around wherever you are and let your eyes rest on one object you care about: a phone, a mug, a photograph, a ring. Look at it the way you'd look at it if you knew this was the last week you'd have it. Notice any tenderness that comes up, and any grip. Then breathe out, and loosen the grip a little, without letting go of the care. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, the One who doesn't pass. The bell holds the time.
False king. Koorh, the false, the passing: king, subjects, palaces, gold and beauty. Without the One, Guru Nanak says, all of it is koorh.
Your line: it won't last. Today, when something you own breaks or something you wanted slips away, say the line, and notice what's still there. Day five hundred forty-eight.

screen: `DAY 548 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN THE HEART IS TRUE.`

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of koorh in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh teaching holds that a householder lives fully in the world while knowing that all of it passes.

match.prompt: koorh, the passing — tap the pairs.

myth: in this salok, koorh only means telling lies
it means what passes, what looks solid and isn't.
Sikhs are asked to leave the world because it is koorh
Guru Nanak was a householder; the point is where the heart leans its full weight.
the salok calls falsehood sweet, like honey
and says it drowns boatloads of people.

fork.setup: the whole world, the salok says, is passing away. what does Guru Nanak ask?
options: with whom should we make friends?
how can we build something that lasts forever?
why should we bother at all?
fork.reveal: with whom should we make friends? the whole world is passing away. the salok ends: without you, all is koorh.

original.note: Gurmukhi: koorh, the false, the unreal, what passes; the opposite of sach, truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: false king means a dishonest ruler.
what it means: koorh is everything that passes, king, gold, body, family, and it's only false when we lean on it instead of the One.
what a scholar hears: koorh pairs with sach, truth, all through the var; Guru Nanak watched the Lodi sultans fall to Babur in his own lifetime.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M1 (koorh raajaa koorh parjaa), Ang 468

notes: The salok is paraphrased; confirm the list (king, subjects, world, mansions and palaces and those who live in them, gold, silver, wearers, body, clothes, beauty, husband and wife), the questions about friendship, honey and drowning boatloads, and the closing plea.
Historical frame: Lodi sultans giving way to Babur (Panipat, 1526) within Guru Nanak's lifetime (1469–1539); confirm.
Guru Nanak as householder at Kartarpur with two sons (Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das) and farming: stated generally; confirm.
